name: Papa (पापा), 56

voice.register: Measured, even and quiet; never raised and never an exclamation mark (chapter 1's one shout is Mausi's). He talks like a platform announcement: an ordered run of whole sentences, each three to eight words with its verb and its full stop, one fact to a sentence, across one to three bubbles, and the last one often names what comes next ('Ab TT aayega.'). That is his long shape, and it is unlike the other long talkers: Mama ji runs on with commas and 'aur haan', Mausi triples and overlaps, Masterji gives a verdict and wanders into cloth and weather; Papa closes each sentence before he starts the next. The everyday fillers of spoken Hindi come into his lines the way they come into anyone's, softly at the head of a sentence ('Suno,' to Mummy, 'Achha?' at a piece of news) or in the middle ('aap bas time bataiye', 'aayenge zaroor'), never as a tag at the end, so the closed announcement stays his. Slow and exact, but not a machine: a time stands where others put a feeling, in the words railway people really say ('do ghante der se', 'baarah minute late'), never a robot count, and good news goes straight to Nani ('Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.'). His only verbless lines are the logged ones, the time correction ('9:40, aaspaas nahin.') and the deed logged in his thanks to the young ('Raat bhar, list ke saath.'), the repeated word when cross ('Koi nahin.'), 'Thank you, ji.' to strangers, and the fixed replies he types. With Nani, who lets him finish, the run is longest (three bubbles); with everyone else it is usually two sentences. Numbers: one of the two people in the cast who lean on them (with Tinku), and only clock times, durations and the count before a noun; never prices, scores or ordinals. Budget: at most one figure a bubble, and at least one bubble in three with none (in the test set below, 3 lines of 12 carry a clock figure and one more says 'do ghante'). Humour is deadpan, about himself and clocks, in the same flat announcement voice.
voice.mix: Careful standard Hindi of the railway colonies, belonging to no one town: full verbs, आप and -इए to elders, no regional colour, and the town's common Hindustani used the way anyone uses it ('fikr mat kijiye', 'zaroor'; cast-wide 8: these words belong to the town, not to Masterji). English comes as single words: the railway nouns every Indian traveller knows (coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket, running status, TT, board; railway people say TT, and 'checker' is an outsider's word) and the everyday nouns of a colony boy grown up (time, battery, alarm, gate, colony, joining, walk); clock times stay figures in all three modes ('9:40'). His verbs are mostly Hindi, many of them the railway's own (gaadi lagna, chhootna, chalna, chart banna, berth milna). The everyday English verb with kar or ho now comes too, where it suits him, and what he turns into one is the booking counter's own work: 'book kiya', 'book kar deta hoon', 'confirm ho gaya', 'cancel karna' (cast-wide 2; Mummy's mark is home things in counter English, 'MCB check karo', so the two still sort apart). He switches by single words, as older speakers do in the Dehradun study the realism notes cite, never by whole English clauses (Mama ji and Mami do that). टिकट is masculine in his mouth ('का टिकट', the standard booking-counter form); if Mama ji's file keeps 'की टिकट' it is Mama ji's colloquial mark and both files say so, otherwise both say 'का'. His late father is 'mere pitaji' | 'मेरे पिताजी' in Hinglish and Hindi alike: plain everyday Hindi with no lean to any community, and what a railway-colony man of 56 says to his Hindi-first mother-in-law ('father' was an outsider's word to her). Hindi mode uses plain Hindi where a low-English reader would stall: 'गाड़ी कहाँ है' for 'running status', 'सैर' for 'walk'. Tamil only in the coach count under his breath, kept in Tamil in every mode (a Tamil reader signs off the words and the script). When cross the English goes altogether: 'late' becomes 'der', 'halt' goes, and only the time stays. 'Darj hai.' | 'Noted.' is his reply to a fact (a PNR, a platform, 'Reached') and, to the young, his thanks as the deed logged ('Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.'); never his thanks for a kindness done for him (Nani's tea gets praise of its timing). His typed messages are English (see typing).
tics: Announces in order: whole sentences, one fact each, each closed with a full stop, the last naming the next step with 'ab ... aayega' or 'ab ... jaayenge' | 'अब ... आएगा' | '... comes next' ('Ab TT aayega.' | 'The TT comes next.'). Only for things that do arrive or go on their own (a train, the TT, the bags going up); a thing he fetches he fetches himself ('Kapda main laata hoon.').
Corrects any vague time to the minute: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, not "around".' He hears 'about', 'around' and 'lagbhag' as errors; quoting the word back is the only time he says it.
The count before the thing: 'Hum solah log hain.' | 'There are sixteen of us.' (Tinku and Mama ji drop number-first).
Names a train by its time: '9:40 wali', '8:15 wali' ('the 9:40'), as railway people do.

A time where others give a feeling, in the words railway people really use: 'do ghante der se', 'baarah minute late', the 9:40 wali; never a robot count ('120 minute') and never a minute stamp on a kindness. Good news is not logged; it goes to Nani at once ('Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.').

Opens a sentence with an everyday filler, softly, as anyone does: 'Suno,' to Mummy (the way Indian couples who use no first names talk), 'Achha?' at news, 'bas' and 'zaroor' in the middle of a request. Never a tag at the end of a line (Tinku's 'haan?', Mama ji's 'aur haan').

Deadpan jokes in the station loudspeaker's frame: 'Kripya dhyan dein.' | 'Attention, please.' then a home fact ('Dal platform number ek par aa chuki hai.', 'Ye chai nahin, sharbat hai.'). At most once a chapter, never while he asks (rule 37), all of it waiting on rulebook Q5.
Never describes a person's temperament; he says what they did.
Counts the coaches under his breath in Tamil as a train comes in: '...naalu, anju, aaru.' (a whisper bubble; proposal, a Tamil reader signs off).
Looks up for a clock before he speaks in any new place (a gesture in the panel, not a word).
When cross: the time left, then one word said twice ('Koi neeche na utre. Koi nahin.'), the guard's flat hand lowered palm down; quieter, never louder, and the English goes.

His judging notes on cards: one time stamp, then the act, in the Hindi transitive past so a note reads the same of a woman or a man; no ordinal and no second figure: '10:20. Asked the coach number again.' | '10:20। फिर से डिब्बे का नंबर पूछा।'; '11:55. Changed seats again.' | '11:55। फिर सीट बदली।'; '1:40. Woke everyone for tea.' | '1:40। चाय के लिए सबको जगाया।'; '12:10. Repacked the bag again.' | '12:10। फिर से बैग बाँधा।'; '9:50. Finished all the snacks.' | '9:50। सारा नाश्ता ख़त्म किया।'; '10:00. Hummed the same tune again.' | '10:00। फिर वही धुन गुनगुनाई।'. Never on a decision whose task the note bears on (rule 20), as often on women as on men, lengths kept even within a decision (story_take.length_faults).
catchphrases: '9:40, aaspaas nahin.' | '9:40, आसपास नहीं।' | '9:40, not "around".' (the correction; his one catchphrase with a number in it, said whenever anyone gives a time with 'around' or 'about' in it; it replaced '9:40, not 9:45.', which held two figures; the owner may keep the old line as a marked exception, since the players' judge picked it)
'Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai.' | 'नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है।' | 'No. The chart has been prepared.' (his final no: once the railway chart is out, nothing changes)

'Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.' | 'आख़िरी डिब्बे तक मैं यहीं हूँ।' | 'I'm here till the last coach goes.' (the platform vigil, the colony-gate boy grown up; the readers marked it true, and Mausa ji's goodbye now leaves before the train moves, so the vigil is Papa's alone)

'Pata nahin, Tinku. / Dal andaaze se banti hai.' | 'पता नहीं, टिंकू। / दाल अंदाज़े से बनती है।' | 'No idea, Tinku. / Dal is done when it tastes right.' (when anyone asks how long the dal takes: the one question the man of minutes answers 'Pata nahin', with the plain words every home cook uses; it replaces the maxim 'Dal ghadi dekhkar nahin banti. Swaad se banti hai.', which read as a made-up saying)
voice.exclamation: 'Kamaal hai.' | 'कमाल है।' | English mode 'Remarkable.' Said flat, with a full stop and never an exclamation mark, a whole sentence that keeps its verb. Two uses: real surprise at good news, which he then carries straight to Nani ('Kamaal hai. Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.'), and dry irony, in two bubbles ('Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat book kiya? / Kamaal hai.'; the power cut that came on time). No religious meaning: 'kamaal' is an everyday word for a wonder or a feat. His alone as an exclamation (Mama ji's 'Kamaal!' went in the matrix, 2.15). The English rendering avoids every mild oath (Gosh, Goodness, Good grief).
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY: plain, said as a fact against himself: what he said, that it was wrong, and where the right answer is: 'Maine 9:40 kaha tha. / Galat nikla. / Board par 9:25 hai.' | 'मैंने 9:40 कहा था। / ग़लत निकला। / बोर्ड पर 9:25 है।' | 'I said 9:40. / I was wrong. / The board says 9:25.' No stamp and no trade word: 'Maine ... kaha tha. Galat nikla.' is how anyone owns a wrong fact ('9:40 mera time tha' was heard as 'it was my turn'). His own past with ने, so nothing marks you. It sorts apart by shape from Mausa ji's subjectless 'Galti hui.', Tinku's 'Sorry, meri galti.' and Mausi's tripled 'sorry'. THANKS, plain and warm: to Nani and the elders, never a register word; he praises the timing of what they did, the highest praise he knows: 'Mummy ji, chai bilkul time par thi.' | 'मम्मी जी, चाय बिल्कुल टाइम पर थी।' | 'Mummy ji, the tea was right on time.'; to you and Tinku, his own shape, the deed logged with no verb about the one he thanks, then the hand-over: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai. / Wo list ab tumhari hai.' | 'रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है। / वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है।' | 'All night, with the list. Noted. / That list is yours now.' (the matrix's '6:00, gate par. Noted.'; 'Bahut achha kiya' is Mummy's); to strangers and the TT, 'Thank you, ji.' | 'थैंक यू, जी।' | 'Thank you, ji.', the plain words people say, his by the whole sentences around it ('Ji, S4 mein solah hain.') and apart from Mami's 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.' by the bare 'ji' ('Dhanyavaad' is announcement Hindi and reads Sanskritised in a person's mouth). WHEN HE IS THANKED: the everyday brush-off, then the next job: 'Roz ka kaam hai. / Ab wapsi ka ticket dekhta hoon.' | 'रोज़ का काम है। / अब वापसी का टिकट देखता हूँ।' | 'It's nothing, I do it every day. / Now for the return tickets.' (no 'Arre': Mummy's thanks reply opens on it, and the matrix gives 'arre' to Captain sahab). By text: 'No need.' and the next job. 'Darj hai.' is never his thanks for a kindness done for him (Nani's tea gets praise of its timing); it logs a fact, or a duty you or Tinku carried, and is 'Noted.' in his typing. LOVE: never said in words. A deed done ahead of time, said as a plain fact ('Didi, neeche ki berth aapki hai. / March mein hi ho gayi thi.'); 'Reached?' typed after any journey you make without him (his alone); standing on the platform till the last coach has gone ('Aakhri dibbe tak main yahin hoon.'), the colony-gate boy grown up; good news carried first to Nani. The nearest he comes to pride is the album's count: 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.'
uses: Clock times in figures, to the minute (9:40, 6:35, 8:55); durations in the words people say (do ghante, das minute, baarah minute late)
ab ... aayega / ab ... jaayenge | अब ... आएगा / अब ... जाएँगे | ... comes next
Sab confirm hai | सब कन्फ़र्म है | All confirmed (his railway praise to the group, at most once a chapter)
Nahin. Chart ban chuka hai | नहीं। चार्ट बन चुका है | No. The chart has been prepared
Kripya dhyan dein | कृपया ध्यान दें | Attention, please (only to open a joke)

Thanks: 'chai bilkul time par thi' (to elders, praise of the timing); the deed logged, then the hand-over: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.' | रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है। | All night, with the list. Noted. (to the young); 'Thank you, ji' | थैंक यू, जी | Thank you, ji (to strangers and the TT)
Being thanked: 'Roz ka kaam hai.' | रोज़ का काम है। | It's nothing, I do it every day, then the next job
Darj hai | दर्ज है | Noted (his reply to a fact, and his thanks to the young as the deed logged; never for a kindness done for him)
Everyday fillers, at the head or in the middle of a sentence: suno (to Mummy), achha, haan, bas; the town's Hindustani: fikr mat kijiye, zaroor

Railway Hindi verbs: gaadi lag gayi (drawn up at the platform), gaadi chhooti, gaadi chal padi, chart ban gaya, berth mil gayi; and the counter's English verbs with kar or ho: book kiya, book kar deta hoon, confirm ho gaya
'9:40 wali' (a train named by its time)

Railway nouns: gaadi, maal gaadi (goods train), dibba and aakhri dibba (coach, the last coach), patri (track), coach, berth, platform, PNR, chart, waiting list, booking, ticket (masculine), TT, running status, board
His past: 'mere pitaji' | मेरे पिताजी, a goods-train guard; colony ka gate; maal gaadi
The dal: dal, andaaze se (by feel, the cook's everyday word), which is how the one untimed thing in his life gets made
Mummy ji, Didi, Bhai sahab, Captain sahab, Masterji (with आप); Tinku (तुम); 'Suno,' to Mummy
never: Vague time words: about, roughly, around, nearly | लगभग, क़रीब, आसपास | lagbhag, kareeb (except quoting the word back in his correction); a script can check his lines for these
'sharp' as a time word: his minute is exact already, and three askers wore the word out

A robot count where people say hours ('120 minute' for two hours), a minute stamp on a family member's kindness ('5:52 par chai...'), or 'Darj hai.' or 'Noted.' as thanks for a kindness done for him (Nani's tea): a register is for parcels, not for Nani. To the young it logs a duty they carried, with no minute stamp ('Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.')
An English verb with kar or ho built on a home thing ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo': Mummy's mark); a whole English clause (Mama ji's and Mami's way)
'jaldi karo' or any 'hurry up': he says the time left instead
'I missed you', 'I'm proud of you', 'love', 'Bahut khushi hui' or any word about his own feelings

Other people's set phrases (the common fillers are free; these are not): Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.', Mausa ji's one-word 'Theek.' and 'Lo.', his lone 'Hmm.' when thanked and his 'Hmm. Baitho.', Nani's 'Bas.' as a closer and 'Khush raho', Masterji's 'Jeete raho' and 'Dekhiye' as an opener, Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!' and 'Shabaash!', Mummy's 'Badhai ho!', her 'Arre, isme kya.' and her 'Bahut achha kiya', Mami's 'Congratulations.', 'Correct?' and 'Tick.', Tinku's 'haan?' tag and 'Sorry, meri galti.', Mama ji's 'aur haan' run-on and 'Don't worry', your 'Pehle ___' and 'Badhiya'; any cricket call ('not out', 'Next ball'); and 'Mubarak ho' (unused for now: it and 'Badhai ho' are both everyday congratulations and take one ruling, and an Urdu-speaking reader checks that both sides are treated alike, India verdict 3)
'checker' for the TT (an outsider's word), and announcement Hindi in his own mouth ('Dhanyavaad'): his railway words are the ones railway people say
Prices or money (Mummy's), scores or cricket words (Tinku's and Captain sahab's), ordinals or numbered items (nobody's in speech)
Two figures in one bubble (the only exception is the Tamil whisper count)
beta, or any word for you that fixes gender (rule 8; rulebook Q7)
A Hindi form that marks your gender: no -ोगे/-ोगी future, no 'pahunch gaye/gayi', no 'thak gaye', no 'kaun jaayega?' (rule 66); questions to you use the subjunctive ('कौन रखे?')
Whether you travel on his pass: the pass rules treat a grown son and a grown daughter differently (rule 8)
A temperament word about anyone: moody, shy, emotional, bossy, lazy

Anything that doubts a report of harassment, of being followed, or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22). Above all his own habit turned on one: no 'Kitne baje?', 'Kab?' or 'time bataiye' asked of a report as if it needs a time to count, and no proof word (saboot, likhit, writing, proof) near a report beat
A rule for choosing in his ask; only the goal of the moment, never the number the two tie on (rule 37); a card person's name or a card note's words in any bubble (rule 36)
A joke while he asks (rule 37); a joke at anyone's cost
Any religious word or exclamation (rule 3): no Hai Ram, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Ishwar; in English mode no Gosh, Goodness, Good grief, Thank God
Slang: chill, bro, scene, whatever
A shout bubble, an exclamation mark, or a year on screen (rules 2 and 35)
address: YOU: तुम only in lines that show no gender (rule 66): commands ('सो लो', 'देखो'), 'who should' asks in the subjunctive ('टीटी के लिए टिकट कौन रखे?'), and lines where you are not the doer ('आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।', 'तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।'). His thanks to you has no verb about you ('रात भर, लिस्ट के साथ। दर्ज है।'). One line falls outside the three shapes: the album's 'इस साल चार बार गाड़ी पकड़ी।', a past with ने where you are the doer and the verb agrees with गाड़ी. It marks no gender, but rule 66 does not name that shape, so the owner either adds 'a past with ने, where the verb agrees with the thing' as a fourth shape or has the native reader clear the line onto the build's cleared list; no wording change if the owner agrees. Possessives agree with the thing, not you ('बर्थ 36 तुम्हारी है', 'वो लिस्ट अब तुम्हारी है'). No name, no beta, no family word; he often opens with the time instead of 'you'. You answer 'Ji Papa' and आप, exactly as you speak to Mummy.

NANI: 'Mummy ji', आप and -इए ('Mummy ji, aap fikr mat kijiye.'). She is the one he talks to most and longest, because she lets him finish, and the one he carries good news to first. Readers confirm the word carries no community lean.

MUMMY: no name and no title; he opens with 'Suno,' or with the time ('Suno, nau baj gaye.'), the way Indian couples who never use first names talk; both say तुम, so the game's own couple carries no honorific-to-husband pattern.
MAMA JI: to his face तुम and no name (the household has no first names); to you he is 'Mama ji'. Mama ji calls him 'Jija ji'.
MAUSI: 'Didi', आप. MAUSA JI: 'Bhai sahab', आप. Both wait on the Hindi-first and South Indian readers (rule 65) and the one family address table.
MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: by their titles, आप.
MAMI: no name, आप (his formality, even to a younger in-law).
A CHILD: commands only ('Gilaas seedha karo.'), so no gender.
STRANGERS AND CARD PEOPLE: आप and 'ji', always; to the TT the count comes first ('Ji, S4 mein solah hain.' | 'जी, S4 में सोलह हैं।') and the thanks is 'Thank you, ji.'
samples: GIVING AN ORDER (the lead-in to the 1.08 ask: the headcount, then the goal of the moment; rule 37, both halves of the twin in this same three-bubble shape): 'There are sixteen of us. / We have only twelve berths. / The train leaves at 9:40.' | 'Hum solah log hain. / Berth sirf baarah hain. / Gaadi chhootne ka time 9:40 hai.' | 'हम सोलह लोग हैं। / बर्थ सिर्फ़ बारह हैं। / गाड़ी छूटने का समय 9:40 है।' (Kept. One figure a bubble. Count before the noun. The third bubble is a station announcement's own shape. No filler and no joke: it is the ask's lead-in.)

ANNOUNCING WHAT COMES NEXT (the train pulls in at the junction): 'The train is in. / S4 is at the front. / Bags go up next.' | 'Gaadi lag gayi hai. / S4 aage hai. / Ab bag upar jaayenge.' | 'गाड़ी लग गई है। / S4 आगे है। / अब बैग ऊपर जाएँगे।' (Kept: the readers marked his whole-sentence announcing true. 'Gaadi lagna' is railway Hindi with a Hindi verb.)

GIVING AN ORDER (the bay at night): 'Bags go under the berths. / Lights go out at ten. / The TT comes next.' | 'Bag berth ke neeche jaayenge. / Batti das baje bujhegi. / Ab TT aayega.' | 'बैग बर्थ के नीचे जाएँगे। / बत्ती दस बजे बुझेगी। / अब टीटी आएगा।' (Kept, with 'TT' for 'checker': a railwayman says TT. 'Batti das baje bujhegi.' rings true. The futures agree with bags, lights and the TT.)

MOVED (1.10: he lays the list on the lower berth, turned to you, taps it twice and takes his hand away): 'My battery has died. / Tonight, you are in charge.' | 'Meri battery khatam hai. / Aaj raat in-charge tum ho.' | 'मेरी बैटरी ख़त्म है। / आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो।' (Kept word for word. You are not the doer of 'इंचार्ज तुम हो'.)

WORRYING (to Mummy on the platform; the refreshing is what kills his battery by ten): 'Listen, the train is twelve minutes late. / Now it is fourteen. / I will check the running status again.' | 'Suno, gaadi baarah minute late hai. / Ab chaudah ho gaye. / Running status phir dekhta hoon.' | 'सुनो, गाड़ी बारह मिनट लेट है। / अब चौदह हो गए। / मैं फिर देखता हूँ, गाड़ी कहाँ है।' ('Suno,' is how he opens to his wife, now that the filler belongs to everyone. Minutes are right here: running status shows minutes. Hindi mode says 'गाड़ी कहाँ है' for a low-English reader. Said to Mummy, not you.)

TEASING (Mama ji on the phone, who has booked the night before again; 'Kamaal hai.' as dry irony): 'You booked tomorrow's train tonight? / Remarkable.' | 'Kal ki gaadi ka ticket aaj raat book kiya? / Kamaal hai.' | 'कल की गाड़ी का टिकट आज रात बुक किया? / कमाल है।' ('Book kiya' is back: the counter's English verb with kar suits a railway clerk (cast-wide 2). टिकट masculine, his standard form.)

TEASING (Captain sahab, at the lane ground on cup day): 'Captain sahab, you said nine o'clock. / I have been here since 8:55.' | 'Captain sahab, aapne nau baje kaha tha. / Main 8:55 se khada hoon.' | 'कप्तान साहब, आपने नौ बजे कहा था। / मैं 8:55 से खड़ा हूँ।' (Kept. One figure a bubble.)

PRAISING (the bay at dawn, nobody missing): 'Everyone is on the train. / Nobody was left behind. / All confirmed.' | 'Sab log gaadi mein hain. / Koi peeche nahin chhoota. / Sab confirm hai.' | 'सब लोग गाड़ी में हैं। / कोई पीछे नहीं छूटा। / सब कन्फ़र्म है।' (His railway praise to the group, at most once a chapter. छूटा agrees with 'koi'.)

PRAISING YOU (the album, in its own panel, never Nani's): 'Four trains this year. / Nobody ever had to remind you.' | 'Is saal chaar baar gaadi pakdi. / Tumhein kabhi yaad nahin dilana pada.' | 'इस साल चार बार गाड़ी पकड़ी। / तुम्हें कभी याद नहीं दिलाना पड़ा।' (The Hindi note's fix: nobody says 'four trains happened'. पकड़ी agrees with गाड़ी and पड़ा is impersonal, so nothing marks you. But you are the unspoken doer of पकड़ी, a past with ने, and rule 66 names only three shapes: the owner adds the ने past whose verb agrees with the thing as a fourth, or the native reader clears this line onto the build's cleared list. No wording change if the owner agrees.)

habits: DEVICE: a plain black smartphone in a plain black case, in his trouser pocket, charged every night at ten; normal text size, since his eyes are good. On the night train it dies by 10 pm because he has refreshed the running status since noon (the worry line's reason, shown plainly, never as an age joke).

SCRIPT: English in Latin letters for everything he types, in all three language modes, because that is how he types and because 'Reached?' marks no gender while 'पहुँच गए?' does (rule 66). Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages too.

SHAPE: he types the way he speaks. Each line is one short whole English sentence with its verb, a capital and a full stop, one fact to a line, in order. Times in figures with a colon (9:40, never 9.40 or 'nine forty').

NUMBERS: the speech budget carried onto the screen: at most one figure a line, and at least one line in three with none ('Charge your phone tonight.'). No prices, no scores, no numbered lists (no '1.', no ticks: Mami's), no ordinals.

FOUR FIXED LINES, his only ones with no full sentence: 'Reached?' (after any journey you make without him; it means 'I missed you'; his alone in the cast), 'Noted.' (his reply to a fact you send, a PNR, a platform, 'Reached'; never to a thank-you), 'No need.' (his reply to a thank-you, followed by the next job), 'Good morning.' (under the 6:35 picture).

FULL STOPS: the family reads them as cross; they are not. The method notes cite NPR's report of a study where a one-word text ending in a full stop read as less sincere. The story can use the misreading once, with Tinku explaining it.
SPEED: one slow forefinger, the phone in his other palm; he rereads before sending; no typos; autocorrect off.

REPLIES: within a minute, always, distinct from Mausa ji's 'Ok.' an hour later. Distinct too from Captain sahab's telegram style with no punctuation, Mummy's and Tinku's lowercase, and Mama ji's and Mausi's doubled marks.
EMOJI AND STICKERS: none. VOICE NOTES: never sends one (he says they have no time in them); he listens to Mausi's in full and replies in text.

FORWARDS: none, except one good-morning picture to the family at 6:35, after the walk with Captain sahab (a sunflower, or a glass of tea on a sunny windowsill; never a lotus, which is a party symbol, never a marigold, which leans to ritual, never a god or a famous face, rule 3) with 'Good morning.' under it. Never politics, never false news, never a forward he has not read. The readers marked the 6:35 flower true.
CALLS: anything that matters is a call, made at the minute he said he would call. Nani gets calls, never texts, and good news reaches her by a call before anyone else.
TIMING: 'Reached?' goes out within ten minutes of your train's due time, by the running status, not the timetable.
ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' label, no group chat (owner, 23 Oct).

He now says 'Suno,' to Mummy, 'Achha?' at news, and 'bas' and 'zaroor' mid-line, always at the head or in the middle of a sentence and never as a tag, so the closed announcement shape still tells him apart.

ENGLISH VERB WITH KAR OR HO (cast-wide 2): allowed where it suits him, and a railway clerk says the booking counter's verbs that way: 'book kiya' is back in the Mama ji tease, and 'Ticket main book kar deta hoon' in moment 3. His everyday verbs stay Hindi railway verbs, and he never turns a home thing into an English verb, which is Mummy's mark.

THANKS (cast-wide 3 and the 'Darj hai' note): 'Darj hai.' is no longer his thanks for a kindness done for him; it stays his reply to a fact ('Noted.' in his typing, which the readers called perfect) and logs a duty the young carried. Thanks to Nani is now the readers' line, praise of the timing: 'Mummy ji, chai bilkul time par thi.', with a second bubble 'Aapko kaise pata tha?'. To the young, his own matrix shape, the deed logged: 'Raat bhar, list ke saath. Darj hai.'; to strangers and the TT 'Thank you, ji.'. When thanked, the everyday brush-off 'Roz ka kaam hai.' then the next job (moment 7), and 'No need.' by text. 'Isme kya' is left to Mausa ji and 'Shabaash' to Mausi, as their notes give them.

SORRY (cast-wide 3): kept as plain owning of a wrong fact, 'Galat nikla.', with no stamp and no trade word; all three modes now say it the way people do, 'Maine 9:40 kaha tha. Galat nikla.' | 'मैंने 9:40 कहा था। ग़लत निकला।' | 'I said 9:40. I was wrong.', in place of the translated '9:40 mera time tha', which was heard as 'it was my turn'. 'Meri galti' was not added, so his sorry stays apart from Tinku's new 'Sorry, meri galti.'

MINUTES INSTEAD OF FEELINGS (real-India note): '120 minute der se' is now 'do ghante der se' (moment 2, the readers' exact fix); the thanks with a 5:52 stamp is gone; the good news is no longer 'Khabar 11:52 par aayi. Darj kar li.' but 'Kamaal hai. Mummy ji ko abhi batata hoon.' (moment 12), so the news goes to Nani, which is his want. The tic now says a time in the words railway people use, never a robot count.

Bahut achha.', so Papa's moment 3 avoids all of those: 'Ye toh bahut achhi baat hai. / Kis din pahunchna hai? Ticket main book kar deta hoon.' RULE 22 (cast-wide 5): the rumour line 'Bina time ke khabar nahin banti.' (no time, no news) was his time habit turned into a demand for proof, one screenshot from 'the family wants proof'. Moment 8 is now 'Achha? Kab se band ho rahi hai, Captain sahab? / Kal subah walk mein udhar se chalenge.', a question and a plan for their walk. The never list now bars his 'Kitne baje?' or 'Kab?' asked of any report, and proof words near a report beat.

The last-coach vigil stays his (the readers marked it true; Mausa ji's note moves his goodbye to before the train moves) and is now a catchphrase. Moment 11 says nothing about 'only water'.

URDU-ROOTED WORDS (cast-wide 8): 'fikr' and 'zaroor' now come to him as the town's ordinary words ('Mummy ji, aap fikr mat kijiye.', 'Mummy ji, aayenge zaroor.'), so they are no longer the tailor's badge.
